attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own article, endorsed.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps his 'I can find no evidence' wording, so it reports the result of his own search. It does not say Microsoft's actual capacity is below a ceiling.

contract.note: Reading it as a report of his own search follows his own qualifier. Public capacity totals cannot test what he personally found, so the axis is correctly not_applicable.

reviews.rationale: The sentence reports Zitron's own search result ('I can find no evidence'), not a checkable claim about how much capacity Microsoft actually added. No independent record of his research exists in the packet. Microsoft's disclosures and outside estimates cannot show what he found. So the claim is untestable as worded.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own article, endorsed.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the $37B and 20M figures, 'mostly', and the 'seems' hedge on the growth part. The hedged growth impression is not scored.

contract.note: Reading 'mostly' as more than half, using the March 2026 quarter, and not scoring the 'seems' clause is an ordinary, fair reading of his words.

evidence.note: Microsoft's Q3 FY26 release confirms the run rate surpassed $37B. This is a company disclosure, and it supports only the headline figure, not OpenAI's share of it.
The Q3 FY26 call remarks confirm more than 20M paid Copilot seats, a figure the contract's support condition names. This is a company disclosure and says nothing about OpenAI's share of AI revenue.

reviews.rationale: Microsoft's own disclosures confirm both headline figures: the $37B run rate and the 20M paid seats. But no item shows what share of the $37B comes from OpenAI compute. That share is the central claim ('mostly'). The packet has no evidence for or against it, so the claim can be neither supported nor contradicted. The 'seems' growth impression is hedged and not scored.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own article, endorsed.

semantics.note: The core is preserved, but 'across the board' and 'or lower, in some cases' were dropped. The proposition also hardens a general typical-range statement into a universal rule, with no exception for completed phases.

contract.note: The contract counts a delivered phase of a larger campus as a completed data center. Zitron did not supply that reading, and in the same piece he disputes counting phases as completion. Treating his typical build range as a strict universal is also stretched against him. The result turns on these readings.

evidence.note: PDG's July 2024 release on Phase One of a 150MW campus. The quoted text confirms energization but does not show the 52MW or 12-month figures. A phase of a larger campus is not clearly a completed data center under a fair reading. Company disclosure.
Epoch's Nov 2025 note predicts the first GW sites coming online in early 2026. It is a forecast and does not verify any operational 1GW site by May 2026.

reviews.rationale: The only contradiction of the build-time clause depends on counting a 52MW phase of a 150MW campus as a completed data center. Zitron did not supply that reading, and the quoted text does not show the 12-month figure. On the gigawatt clause, e2 is only a forecast; no item verifies or rules out an operational 1GW site by publication. Under a fair reading, the packet does not settle either clause.
